body: The pre-registered outcomes for the evaluation should be few and hard: low-risk cesarean rate, severe maternal morbidity, preterm birth, first-trimester enrollment, share of births with a midwife and a doula present, share of births occurring in a facility without a planned attendant, cost per pregnancy episode through twelve months, and patient-reported experience. If by month 36 the cesarean rate has not fallen below 40% and cost per episode has not fallen, the payment design is wrong and should be changed; the evaluation exists to force that conversation rather than to decorate a report.
A plan that cannot describe its own failure modes has not been thought through. Eight are identified here, each with the evidence that makes it plausible and the design feature meant to contain it.

The midwifery workforce does not materialize. Licensing a profession does not create it. If the education partnership stalls, international recruitment runs into immigration walls, and hospitals deny privileges as Minnesota's did for years, Tier 0 defaults to prenatal nurses under physician protocols and Tier 1 never opens. The containment is to make privileges and coverage statutory rights rather than negotiated favors, to fund preceptorship directly, to pursue three sources of midwives at once (local education, mainland compact licensees, international equivalency), and to design Tier 0 so that it delivers value with nurses alone while midwives are built.

Consolidation happens and readiness does not. The hospitals close, the hubs are designated, and the readiness layer is the line item that gets cut, leaving the unplanned birth in an unready emergency department, which is precisely where Kozhimannil's data locate the harm [57]. The containment is to fund readiness first, before designation, through the administrative order in month one, and to make readiness a condition of every hospital's license rather than a grant program.

Payment reform produces a null result. Arkansas, Tennessee, Minnesota, and the Netherlands all reformed maternity payment and none moved cesareans or outcomes [38][55][61][62]. The containment is that this design does not rely on payment alone: the evidence-backed lever is public, physician-level measurement combined with mandatory second opinion, and the payment change exists to remove the incentive that would otherwise fight the measurement. If the dashboard is delayed or anonymized under pressure, the plan is in trouble, and that is the political fight worth having.

The doula benefit exists and nobody uses it. This is the modal outcome in the states [46]. The containment is a rate high enough to sustain a workforce, direct enrollment through the Maternity Home, a statutory right of access to the delivery room, and a locally trained corps rather than an imported one.

Out-of-hospital birth scales before integration and a first baby dies. The Oregon experience is the warning [43]. The containment is the sequencing: no Community Maternity Unit opens before the licensing statute, the transfer agreements, and the tele-obstetric hub exist; first births are steered to alongside units; and every out-of-hospital birth is in the data system from day one.

The hospital association and the medical college block the statute. They have blocked every transparency bill so far. The containment is to route the first year through ASES contracting and the Departamento de Salud's licensing authority, so that the measures with the strongest evidence do not depend on legislation, and to make the hub capacity payment attractive enough that the hospitals most likely to be designated become supporters of the consolidation they would otherwise fight.

The Medicaid cliff arrives and the program is the first casualty. If the 2027 allotment is not extended, Plan Vital loses a quarter to a half of its federal money and every discretionary program is at risk. The containment is that this architecture lowers cost per birth and is therefore the version of maternity care that survives austerity; the paper recommends framing it in Washington as a cliff mitigation measure, and building the highest-return components (mode-neutral payment, Robson reporting, readiness, the home kit) so early that they are embedded before the cliff.

The technology is bought and sits in a drawer. Ultrasound probes without a billing code, blood pressure cuffs without a nurse hub, plasma without a hemorrhage protocol, and satellite dishes without a maintenance contract all become inventory. The containment is that no device is procured in this plan without its payment path, its clinical protocol, and its staffing named in the same procurement document.

sections.h1: 10. What Must Be Verified Before Committing Money
body: The research behind this paper was thorough within the limits of public sources, and several primary sources were unreachable. The following items are stated in the body as unverified or estimated and should be resolved, mostly by ASES and the Departamento de Salud from records they already hold, before the budget in Section 5 is treated as anything more than an order of magnitude.

list: The actual global obstetric fee and per-delivery facility payment under Plan Vital and each managed-care organization, by mode of delivery, and the current APR-DRG relative weights for vaginal and cesarean birth. This is the single most important missing number.
Whether Plan Vital has adopted twelve-month postpartum coverage, and if not, the cost of doing so under the capped allotment.
The rate, enrollment mechanism, and utilization of the doula benefit that March of Dimes reports as active.
The number of nurse-midwives licensed under Ley 254-2015 and practicing, and the status of any midwifery licensing bill in SUTRA.
A consistent OBGYN headcount series from the Junta de Licenciamiento or AAMC to quantify attrition since 2010.
The Maternal Mortality Review Committee's case-level findings for 2019–2024: pregnancy-related versus pregnancy-associated deaths, causes, and preventability.
The current list of labor-and-delivery units and neonatal levels by hospital, including the disputed status of Pavía Arecibo and the opening status and staffing plan of the Vieques hospital.
Obstetric malpractice premiums and claim frequency from SIMED and other carriers.
Dollar amounts and current status of Title V, Healthy Start, MIECHV, and any HRSA maternal health awards in Puerto Rico, and whether Puerto Rico administers its Conrad 30 allocation.
Whether Act 60 Chapter 2 physician decrees are currently being issued at all, and the Fiscal Oversight Board's position on a narrow reopening.
Vaginal birth after cesarean, low birthweight, and vital-statistics teen birth rates from the NCHS final data tables.
Annual abortion counts and the operating status of the four remaining clinics under Leyes 122-2025, 183-2025, and 18-2026.
Which provisions of the 2025 federal reconciliation law, if any, apply to Puerto Rico's Medicaid program.

body: The estimates in Table 3 rest on the following stated assumptions. Each is a defensible starting point drawn from the sources cited in the body and should be replaced with Puerto Rico claims and payroll data as soon as ASES releases them.

Births are assumed at 18,000 a year falling toward 15,000; steady-state figures use 18,000 to be conservative on cost. Plan Vital's share of births is 66%. A caseload midwife carries 35 to 40 births a year at a loaded cost of $150,000, so 40% midwife-led care at 18,000 births requires about 200 midwives; because each midwife-led pregnancy displaces roughly $2,000–2,400 of physician prenatal and delivery fees, the net cost of the midwifery workforce is about half its gross cost [39]. Doula uptake is assumed at 60% at $1,500, well above the mainland experience, on the assumption that direct enrollment and a right of access are enforced. The home kit is $150 in hardware per pregnancy with a 25-person nurse hub. Hub capacity payments of $1.5–2.5 million are sized to the locum-equivalent cost of a 24-hour obstetric hospitalist line ($1.3–1.5 million at about $3,900 per shift) plus a share of anesthesia and neonatal standby [85]. Community Maternity Units are assumed to run at $2.5–3 million each with $1–1.5 million recovered in facility payments. The cesarean offset assumes a 20-point reduction on 18,000 births at $2,000–4,000 per avoided case, consistent with the MACPAC facility differential and the Strong Start birth-cost gap [39][42]. The birth-center pathway offset applies the Strong Start first-year saving of $2,010 to 3,000 low-risk births. Nurse home visiting is costed at a $5,000 per family annual pro-ration of the WSIPP total program cost [92]. Technology capital assumes 100 ultrasound kits at $6,000 including training and 40 resilience kits at $50,000. The Commonwealth share is computed at 24% of the Plan Vital portion through FY2027 and 45% thereafter [19].
